name: Matific
line: Matific teaches in short games at one learning level. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Matific: Matific teaches in short games at one learning level. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Matific teaches through short game-like activities on one concept, keeps one learning level for each student, and goes back to earlier grades when it detects a gap [2][3]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Matific starts a student at a learning level that is, by default, the grade of the class, and a parent can change it [3][6]. Teachers can set assessments in place of its automatic placement test [7].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, each problem carries what a learner needs: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer after it is answered, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Matific the unit is the episode: a game-like activity of 5 to 15 minutes on one concept [2], about five questions that rise in challenge [4]. Students earn stars for their performance in each activity [5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [18].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. Matific keeps one learning level for each student [3]. On its Adventure Island, Matific's AI chooses activities around that level, to close gaps or add challenge [3][8].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Matific's mastery report, which is in beta, marks a topic mastered when the student is judged likely to earn 4 or more stars on its activities [11]. A student moves to the next grade after completing all the material for the current one [3].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Matific goes back to work from earlier grades when its algorithm detects a gap [3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [19].

rows.start: One learning level, by default the grade of the class [3]. A parent can change it [6]. Teachers can set assessments in place of its placement test [7].
rows.teaching: Game-like activities of 5 to 15 minutes on one concept [2], with instructions, hints and feedback [10].
rows.next: On Adventure Island, its AI chooses activities to close gaps or add challenge [8]. In the Training Zone, the student picks the skill [9].
rows.mastery: A topic counts as mastered when the student is judged likely to earn 4 or more stars on its activities [11].
rows.review: Work from earlier grades when its algorithm detects a gap [3].
rows.print: Printable worksheets in its activity library; not all can be printed yet [12].
rows.adult: Teachers assign activities and worksheets [2]. In a case study, results depended on how teachers built it into lessons [4].
rows.reports: A parent report and dashboard [13]. For teachers, real-time analytics [14] and a mastery report, in beta [11].
rows.evidence: One 2017 quasi-experiment, grades 2 and 3: effect size 0.19 on a district test, low-use classes excluded [2]. No Evidence for ESSA rating [16].

theirs: Matific is a game-based math program for ages 4 to 15, kindergarten through grade 9 [1]. Work comes in episodes: game-like activities of 5 to 15 minutes on one concept [2], each about five questions that rise in challenge [4]. Students earn stars for their performance in each activity [5].

Matific keeps one learning level for each student, by default the grade of the class [3]. On Adventure Island, its AI picks the next activities around that level [3][8]. In the Training Zone, students choose a skill and set the difficulty [9].
credit: Learning through play, in short activities, from age 4 [1][2].
Instructions, hints and feedback inside each activity [10].
A study with a comparison group found a positive effect in grades 2 and 3 [2].

theirs: The one Matific study with a comparison group we found is a 2017 evaluation by SEG Measurement in Hampton City Schools, Virginia [2]. About 1,477 second and third graders took part, and 1,056 with fall and spring scores were analysed, in classes that used Matific and classes that did not, on a 20-item district test. It was not randomized. Classes that completed fewer than 80 episodes were dropped from the Matific group. Adjusted scores were 77.23 for the Matific classes and 73.67 for the others, an effect size of 0.19 overall. The grade 3 effect was significant only at the 10% level [2]. The report does not say who paid for it, and Matific hosts it.

A case study by Attard of Western Sydney University, sponsored by Slate Science, followed 16 teachers in eight primary schools with topic tests before and after [4]. Students gained 34% of the available marks. There was no comparison group, and the report says it cannot say how much of the gain Matific caused [4]. Matific's research page also lists pilots, teacher surveys and small classroom studies from many countries, several with no comparison group [15].
Evidence for ESSA lists Matific without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [16]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report on Matific [17].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 across 55 studies [18]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks, on the researchers' own test a month later [19]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is young and learns best through short math games.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or needs one program from counting through precalculus.
You want printed practice made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Matific?
questions.answer: Matific teaches in short game-like activities at one learning level for each student, and goes back to earlier grades when it detects a gap [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem in that part of math, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Matific work?
questions.answer: Its one study with a comparison group, a 2017 quasi-experiment in grades 2 and 3, found an effect of 0.19 standard deviations on a district test, counting only classes that met a usage target [2]. It was not randomized. Evidence for ESSA lists Matific without a rating [16].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
